title: Four kinds of devotees
hookLine: people come to God in trouble, in curiosity, in need, and in knowing; the Gita calls all four noble
carry: all who come to God are noble

lines: A MOTHER. A STUDENT. A SHOPKEEPER.
cards: Walk into a temple on any evening and look at the faces. A mother whose son is in the hospital. A student the night before an exam.

A man whose shop isn't doing well, asking for a better year. A teenager who's just curious what all this is. An old woman who's been coming every day for sixty years and doesn't seem to need anything at all.
Some people might say only one of them is here for the right reason. The Gita, chapter seven, looks at the same crowd, and says something more generous.

teach.b: First, the problem. The world is bewildered by the three gunas, Krishna says, the three strands of nature, and so it doesn't see him beyond them. His power of illusion is hard to cross, but those who turn to him cross it.
Then verse sixteen. Four kinds of good people turn to me, Arjuna. The arta: the one in distress.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO WANTS TO KNOW.
teach.b: The jijnasu: the one who wants to know.
The artharthi: the one who seeks something, wealth, security, a good outcome.
And the jnani: the one who knows. The mother, the teenager, the shopkeeper, the old woman. Here's what's striking.

All four are called good people, and verse eighteen calls all of them noble: udara, generous, large-hearted. Nobody gets turned away for coming in trouble or coming with a request. But one stands out.

The one who knows, verse seventeen says, always united, devoted to one alone, is the best. I am very dear to that one, and that one is dear to me. Verse eighteen goes further: the one who knows is my very self.

And verse nineteen describes the journey there. At the end of many births, the one who knows takes refuge in me, seeing that Vasudeva is everything. Such a great soul, Krishna says, is very hard to find.
So the ladder isn't a test you pass or fail. You can come in scared, or curious, or asking for a job. The door is open.
And the Gita keeps walking you toward the fourth.

how: Hindu temples welcome people who come for every reason: prayers in illness or trouble, questions, requests for success or a good year, and daily worship with no request at all; Gita 7.16 is often cited to honor all of them.

o: a seeker who's curious to learn more
a devotee who truly knows, dearest to Krishna
a scholar who has memorized the Vedas

games.q: who's who among the four — tap the pairs.
p: the one who wants to know

s: the Gita says coming to God for help in trouble is wrong
the one in distress is one of the four good people, and verse 18 calls all four noble.
Krishna calls the one who knows 'my very self'
verse 18: the one who knows is his very self.
verse 19 says the one who knows arrives quickly and easily
at the end of many births, and such a great soul is very hard to find.

games.q: four people come to worship: one in trouble, one curious, one asking for something, one who knows. which ones does verse 18 call noble?
games.why: all four: udarah, noble. then Krishna says the one who knows is dearest, his very self.

practice: Ask yourself honestly which of the four you are today: here in some kind of trouble, out of curiosity, wanting something to change, or just to be here? There's no wrong answer; the Gita calls all four noble.
Breathe with whatever you found, then, for the last part of the sit, let the reason go and simply sit, as the one who doesn't need anything.

wordCard.voice: Jnani. The one who knows, the fourth and dearest of four kinds of devotees: the one in distress, the one who wants to know, the one who seeks something, and the one who knows. All four noble.

orig.note: Sanskrit: jnani, the one who knows; the fourth and dearest of the four kinds of devotees (7.16–18).

carryVoice: Your line: all who come to God are noble. Whatever brought you to the door, it's open. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 7.13–7.15 (the gunas; maya hard to cross)
Bhagavad Gita 7.16–7.19 (the four kinds of devotees)
